title: Progressive Electricity Billing
statement: Calculate household electricity bills using progressive consumption slabs, a fixed charge, a surcharge, and an on-time rebate. Compare a chronological sequence of monthly bills, identify increases greater than a specified threshold, and report every month tied for the highest bill.
objectives: Apply progressive slabs without charging all units at the highest rate.
Use conditional rules for surcharge, rebate, and unusual bill increases.
Store monthly records as tuples in a list and unpack them during processing.
Preserve exact paise amounts while calculating and rounding charges.
assumptions: The supplied brief gives no tariff values. The following rates are classroom assumptions, not an electricity provider's tariff.
Accept 1-12 months in chronological order, with unique labels of 1-12 characters. Labels are compared without regard to case. Units are nonnegative whole kWh.
The first 100 units cost Rs 1.50 each, the next 100 cost Rs 2.50 each, and every unit above 200 costs Rs 4.00. Fixed charge: Rs 50.00 per month, including at zero consumption.
Consumption above 300 units incurs a surcharge of 10% of the energy charge. At 100 units or less, on-time payment earns a rebate of 5% of the energy charge.
Money is calculated in integer paise. Percentage charges are rounded half up to the nearest paise using (amount * rate + 50) // 100. Only display formatting converts to rupees.
An unusual increase is strictly greater than 25% of the preceding final bill. Exactly 25% does not trigger an alert. There is no alert for the first month.
Malformed month records are retried and do not consume a month slot. Highest-bill ties retain input order.
input: First enter the month count. Then enter label|units|Y/N for each month. Y means payment by the due date. Example: Jan|100|Y.
output: An itemized monthly bill, percentage change from the preceding month, alert labels, total billed amount, and all highest-bill month labels.
thinking: Decomposition: separate input validation, energy slabs, adjustments, and trend reporting.
Pattern recognition: each month follows the same tariff calculation.
Abstraction: represent a month by only its label, consumption, and on-time flag.
Algorithm design: scan the chronological list once, keeping the previous bill and the running maximum.
algorithm: Read and validate the month count.
Read each three-field record. Validate the label, units, and Y/N flag; retry invalid or duplicate records.
Store accepted records as (label, units, on_time) tuples.
For each month, calculate energy in paise using the three progressive slabs.
Calculate the applicable surcharge and rebate, round each to paise, and add the fixed charge.
Print the bill. From the second month onward, calculate percentage change and flag bill * 100 > previous_bill * 125.
Accumulate the grand total and maintain the highest bill and every tied label.
Print the total, highest-bill labels, and unusual-increase labels.
pseudocode:
START
READ a valid month_count in 1..12
months <- empty list; labels <- empty list
WHILE accepted months < month_count
    READ label, units, on_time
    IF record is invalid OR label already exists
        PRINT error; RETRY
    ELSE
        APPEND (label, units, on_time) to months
        APPEND normalized label to labels
previous_bill <- 0; highest_bill <- -1; total <- 0
FOR EACH (label, units, on_time) IN months
    IF units <= 100
        energy <- units * 150
    ELSE IF units <= 200
        energy <- 15000 + (units - 100) * 250
    ELSE
        energy <- 40000 + (units - 200) * 400
    surcharge <- 0; rebate <- 0
    IF units > 300: surcharge <- (energy * 10 + 50) DIV 100
    IF units <= 100 AND on_time = Y
        rebate <- (energy * 5 + 50) DIV 100
    bill <- energy + 5000 + surcharge - rebate
    PRINT itemized bill
    IF previous_bill > 0
        PRINT (bill - previous_bill) * 100 / previous_bill
        IF bill * 100 > previous_bill * 125: RECORD alert
    UPDATE highest bill and all ties
    total <- total + bill; previous_bill <- bill
PRINT total, highest-bill months, alert months
STOP
conclusion: The solution combines progressive arithmetic, conditional policies, and a running comparison without advanced Python features. Its boundary tests distinguish slab transitions, the 300-unit surcharge threshold, paise rounding, and an increase of exactly 25%.

Apply slabs; add fixed charge\nApply surcharge and rebate\nRound adjustments to paise
Print bill; compare with previous\nFlag increase strictly above 25%\nUpdate total and highest-bill ties
Print totals, highest-bill months,\nand unusual increases

title: ATM Transaction Sequence Simulation
statement: Simulate a sequence of deposits and withdrawals against one account. Validate each attempted transaction, enforce withdrawal limits and a minimum balance, leave balances unchanged for rejected attempts, and produce a transaction-by-transaction audit and final reconciliation.
objectives: Maintain an account balance across a sequential transaction list.
Apply multiple validation and withdrawal conditions in a defined order.
Reject repeated transaction identifiers without double-processing an amount.
Reconcile the opening balance, deposits, withdrawals, and closing balance.
assumptions: This is a one-day classroom simulation using fictional data and whole rupees. It does not connect to a bank.
Opening balance is at least Rs 500. Accept 1-50 attempted transactions. Deposits have no policy cap and must be positive whole rupees.
Withdrawal amounts must be positive multiples of Rs 100, no more than Rs 10000 per transaction, and no more than Rs 20000 in successful withdrawals during the day.
Every successful withdrawal must leave at least Rs 500. A later deposit does not reset the daily withdrawal allowance.
A transaction ID is 1-12 ASCII letters or digits, normalized to uppercase. A well-formed row with a syntactically valid new ID reserves that ID even when its type or amount is later rejected.

D means deposit and W means withdrawal; letter case is normalized. Invalid records count as attempts. The first failure in the program's validation order is reported, and rejected records never change the balance.
input: Enter opening balance, number of attempts, then ID|D/W|amount for each attempt. Example: T1|W|1000.
output: For every attempt: ID, acceptance or rejection reason, and unchanged or updated balance. The summary shows counts, deposit and withdrawal totals, and an arithmetic reconciliation.
thinking: Decomposition: validate setup, identify transactions, apply account rules, and reconcile.
Pattern recognition: every accepted transaction changes the same balance state.
Abstraction: retain identifiers, operation types, amounts, and resulting balances.
Algorithm design: process in input order because earlier operations affect later eligibility.
algorithm: Read a valid opening balance and transaction attempt count.
Initialize balance, deposit and withdrawal totals, counters, seen IDs, and audit results.
Read a transaction. Check its shape, ID syntax, and whether that ID has already appeared.
Reserve a new valid ID, then validate type and positive integer amount.
For withdrawals, check denomination, per-transaction limit, daily limit, and remaining balance in that order.
If valid, update balance and the relevant total. Otherwise record a rejection without altering money.
Append the ID, status, and resulting balance to the audit list.
After all attempts, print the audit and verify opening + deposits - withdrawals = final balance.
pseudocode:
START
READ opening_balance >= 500 and attempt_count in 1..50
balance <- opening_balance
seen_ids <- empty list; results <- empty list
deposited <- 0; withdrawn <- 0
accepted <- 0; rejected <- 0
FOR EACH attempt
    READ ID, type, amount
    reason <- empty
    VALIDATE record shape, ID syntax, and uniqueness
    IF new valid ID: ADD ID to seen_ids
    VALIDATE type in {D, W} and positive whole amount
    IF type = W AND no earlier error
        CHECK amount MOD 100 = 0
        CHECK amount <= 10000
        CHECK withdrawn + amount <= 20000
        CHECK balance - amount >= 500
    IF no error
        IF type = D
            balance <- balance + amount
            deposited <- deposited + amount
        ELSE
            balance <- balance - amount
            withdrawn <- withdrawn + amount
        accepted <- accepted + 1
    ELSE
        rejected <- rejected + 1
    APPEND (ID, status or first error, balance) to results
PRINT results, counts, and totals
PRINT opening_balance + deposited - withdrawn = balance
STOP
conclusion: The program demonstrates how ordered validation protects a changing state. Tests confirm exact withdrawal limits, the minimum-balance boundary, rejected-ID reuse, and the fact that deposits do not replenish the daily withdrawal allowance.

Read the next ID | type | amount
Valid format, new ID,\ntype and positive amount?
Record first rejection reason\nKeep balance unchanged
Apply deposit or withdrawal\nUpdate successful totals and count
Append status and resulting balance\nto the transaction audit
Print audit, counts and totals\nOpening + deposits - withdrawals\n= closing balance

title: Warehouse Inventory Reconciliation
statement: Compare opening stock, receipts, dispatches, and physically observed closing stock for multiple products. Identify shortages and surpluses, reject impossible stock movement, and calculate each product's replenishment quantity against its target.
objectives: Reconcile theoretical and physical stock using a stock-balance equation.
Distinguish invalid movement from an auditable physical discrepancy.
Calculate replenishment from the observed stock level.
Store and unpack multi-field product tuples and summarize audit counts.
assumptions: Accept 1-20 attempted product records. All quantities are nonnegative whole units of the same product; cross-product replenishment totals count units only.
Product codes contain 1-12 ASCII letters or digits and normalize to uppercase. The first correctly shaped record with a valid code reserves that code, even if later numeric validation fails.
Expected closing stock = opening + incoming - dispatched. Dispatch greater than opening + incoming is impossible under this model and is rejected.
Difference = observed closing - expected closing. A negative difference is a shortage; a positive one is a surplus.
Observed stock may differ from the records and remains auditable even if it exceeds expected stock. Replenishment is target - observed when observed is below target, otherwise zero.
Invalid records count as attempts and contribute to neither stock calculations nor replenishment totals.
input: Enter the record count, then code|opening|incoming|dispatched|observed_closing|target. Example: P100|50|20|40|28|40.
output: Rejected-record reasons, expected and observed quantities, signed discrepancies, status, per-product replenishment, and audit totals.
thinking: Decomposition: check record validity, calculate expected stock, compare, and replenish.
Pattern recognition: each product follows the same inventory-balance equation.
Abstraction: physical and book quantities are separate fields; neither overwrites the other.
Algorithm design: exclude invalid records before calculating the accepted-record summary.
algorithm: Read a valid record count and initialize products, seen codes, and rejection count.
Read six fields per attempted record and validate the product code and uniqueness.
Validate five nonnegative integer quantities.
Reject dispatch above available stock; otherwise store the product tuple.
For each stored tuple, calculate expected stock and observed - expected.
Classify each difference as shortage, surplus, or match.
Calculate replenishment from observed stock and add it to the total.
Print the itemized audit, discrepancy count, rejected count, and replenishment total.
pseudocode:
START
READ record_count in 1..20
products <- empty list; seen_codes <- empty list
FOR EACH attempted record
    READ code, opening, incoming, dispatched, observed, target
    VALIDATE six fields and a new valid normalized code
    RESERVE each new syntactically valid code
    VALIDATE all quantities as nonnegative integers
    IF dispatched > opening + incoming: REJECT
    IF valid: APPEND the six-field product tuple
    ELSE: PRINT reason and increment rejected count
discrepancies <- 0; total_replenishment <- 0
FOR EACH product tuple
    expected <- opening + incoming - dispatched
    difference <- observed - expected
    IF difference < 0: status <- SHORTAGE
    ELSE IF difference > 0: status <- SURPLUS
    ELSE: status <- MATCH
    IF difference != 0: discrepancies <- discrepancies + 1
    replenish <- 0
    IF observed < target: replenish <- target - observed
    total_replenishment <- total_replenishment + replenish
    PRINT code, expected, observed, difference, status, replenish
PRINT audit and replenishment totals
STOP
conclusion: The audit keeps stock-record discrepancies separate from purchasing needs. Tests show that replenishment uses the physical count, that complete dispatch is valid, and that impossible movement and duplicate codes cannot distort totals.

Read six product fields\nReserve a new valid-shaped code
New valid code, whole quantities,\nand dispatch <= available?
For each accepted tuple:\nexpected = opening + incoming - dispatch\ndifference = observed - expected
Classify shortage / surplus / match\nReplenish only when observed < target\nAccumulate discrepancy and unit totals

title: Multi-Day Water Tank Simulation
statement: Simulate a tank across a sequence of intervals with changing inflow and demand. Keep the stored level within capacity, measure overflow and unmet demand, identify the first interval in which a threshold is reached, and verify the water balance.
objectives: Update a bounded state across multiple time intervals.
Distinguish demand, delivered water, spilled water, and shortage.
Detect threshold crossings before an interval's later withdrawal.
Check conservation using initial water, inflow, final water, supply, and spill.
assumptions: All values are whole litres. Capacity is positive; initial level and threshold lie between zero and capacity, inclusive. Accept 1-30 valid intervals.
Within each interval, all inflow occurs first, excess immediately spills, and demand is then supplied from the remaining stored water. There is no simultaneous-flow model.
Delivered water is the smaller of demand and stored water after filling. Unmet demand is demand minus delivered water.

The threshold means a stored level greater than or equal to the target. Check the initial level and the level after filling, before demand. A later fall below the threshold does not erase the first crossing.
Interval 0 denotes an initially met threshold. A zero threshold is therefore reached initially.
Malformed inflow/demand records are retried and do not advance time. There are no unrecorded leaks or evaporation.
input: Enter capacity, initial level, threshold, interval count, then inflow|demand for each interval. Example: 60|40.
output: A table of start level, inflow, demand, delivered quantity, spill, shortage, and end level; aggregate flows; first threshold interval; and a conservation equation.
thinking: Decomposition: fill, spill, test the threshold, supply demand, and summarize.
Pattern recognition: the same state transition repeats each interval.
Abstraction: represent water as a scalar level and retain an interval tuple for the audit.
Algorithm design: enforce operation order so overflow and shortage can both occur in one interval.
algorithm: Validate capacity, initial water, threshold, and interval count.
Set the current level to initial water and record interval 0 if the threshold is already met.
Read and validate inflow and demand, retrying malformed records.
Save the starting level, add inflow, calculate any spill, and cap the stored level at capacity.
If no earlier crossing exists and the filled level meets the threshold, record the current interval.
Deliver demand up to the available level, calculate shortage, and subtract delivered water.
Accumulate totals and append the interval audit tuple.
After all intervals, print the audit and confirm initial + inflow = final + delivered + spill.
pseudocode:
START
READ valid capacity, initial, threshold, interval_count
level <- initial; first_crossing <- NOT_REACHED
IF initial >= threshold: first_crossing <- 0
INITIALIZE totals and interval records
WHILE completed intervals < interval_count
    READ inflow and demand
    IF either is not a nonnegative integer: PRINT error; RETRY
    start_level <- level
    level <- level + inflow
    spill <- 0
    IF level > capacity
        spill <- level - capacity
        level <- capacity
    IF first_crossing is NOT_REACHED AND level >= threshold
        first_crossing <- current interval number
    served <- demand; shortage <- 0
    IF demand > level
        served <- level
        shortage <- demand - level
    level <- level - served
    UPDATE flow totals
    APPEND (start, inflow, demand, served, spill, shortage, level)
PRINT interval audit and totals
PRINT initial crossing, first interval, or never
PRINT initial + total_inflow = level + total_served + total_spill
STOP
conclusion: The simulation accounts for every litre and makes the order of events explicit. Tests cover initial and zero thresholds, a never-reached threshold, and an interval that spills water before later suffering a shortage.

Set current level and totals\nIf initial >= threshold, record interval 0
Save start level and add inflow
If above capacity: record spill\nand cap the stored level
Record first threshold crossing\nif filled level >= threshold
Supply demand up to available level\nRecord shortage and subtract supply
Print audit, first crossing and totals\nCheck water conservation

title: Student Timetable Conflict Detection
statement: Validate a proposed timetable for one student. Parse course sessions from strings into tuples, detect overlapping sessions and simultaneous room bookings, identify sessions scheduled during room closures, and report whether the timetable is valid.
objectives: Parse and validate strict 24-hour time strings using basic string operations.
Represent sessions and room closures as tuples with minute-based time intervals.
Use nested loops to compare unique session pairs.
Distinguish student conflicts, room conflicts, malformed records, and blocked bookings.
assumptions: Accept 1-20 attempted session records for one student's timetable. Valid days are MON-FRI and valid rooms are R101, R102, and LAB2.
Assumed closures: LAB2 on WED from 10:00 to 12:00, and R102 on FRI from 13:00 to 14:00.
Course codes contain 1-12 ASCII letters or digits. Course, day, and room text normalize to uppercase.
Times use exactly HH:MM, from 00:00 through 23:59. Each session ends after it starts on the same day. Overnight sessions and 24:00 are outside this model.
Intervals are half-open: [start, end). A session may end exactly when another begins or a closure starts. Overlap requires a_start < b_end and b_start < a_end.
Every same-day overlapping pair is a student conflict; it is additionally a room conflict if both rooms match. Compare each pair once.
Identical session tuples are rejected. A course may have distinct sessions. Syntactically valid sessions during closures remain in the pairwise audit so every problem is reported.
Any rejected record, student conflict, or blocked booking makes the complete timetable invalid.
input: Enter the number of attempts and then course|day|HH:MM|HH:MM|room. Example: CS101|MON|09:00|10:00|R101.
output: Rejected-record reasons, unavailable-room bookings, named conflict pairs, separate conflict counts, and a final VALID or INVALID verdict.
thinking: Decomposition: parse sessions, check closures, compare pairs, and combine findings.
Pattern recognition: the same strict overlap test applies to sessions and closures.
Abstraction: replace clock strings with minutes after midnight.
Algorithm design: compare index pairs with the second index greater than the first to avoid double-counting.
algorithm: Define valid days, rooms, and the supplied classroom closure tuples.
Read a valid session count and validate each five-field record.
Convert both valid HH:MM strings into hour * 60 + minute; require start < end.
Reject duplicate session tuples; store other valid tuples.
Compare each stored session with every closure for its room and day, reporting overlaps.
Compare each unique pair of stored sessions on the same day using the strict overlap inequalities.
Count every overlapping pair as a student conflict and, when rooms match, as a room conflict.
Print counts and declare the timetable valid only when no rejection, overlap, or blocked booking exists.
pseudocode:
START
DEFINE valid days, rooms, and closure tuples
READ session_count in 1..20
sessions <- empty list; rejected <- 0
FOR EACH attempted record
    READ course, day, start_text, end_text, room
    VALIDATE fields, course code, day, and room
    FOR EACH of the two time strings
        CHECK exactly HH:MM, ASCII digits, hour 0..23, minute 0..59
        CONVERT to hour * 60 + minute
    CHECK start < end and tuple not already in sessions
    IF valid: APPEND (course, day, start, end, room)
    ELSE: PRINT reason; increment rejected
FOR EACH session AND EACH room closure
    IF same room and day AND start < closure_end AND end > closure_start
        REPORT unavailable booking
FOR first_index FROM 0 TO number_of_sessions - 1
    FOR second_index FROM first_index + 1 TO number_of_sessions - 1
        IF same day AND first_start < second_end AND second_start < first_end
            REPORT student conflict
            IF rooms match: ALSO COUNT room conflict
PRINT counts
IF no rejected records, student conflicts, or blocked bookings
    PRINT VALID
ELSE: PRINT INVALID
STOP
conclusion: Converting times to minutes makes the conflict rule precise and reusable. Tests prove that adjacent sessions and closure endpoints are allowed, that different rooms do not remove a student's conflict, and that duplicate records do not multiply pair counts.

Read course | day | start | end | room
Valid fields, times and duration;\nnot an identical session?
Convert times to minutes\nAppend the session tuple
Compare sessions with closures\nSame room/day and strict overlap\nReport unavailable bookings
Compare each unique session pair\nSame-day overlap = student conflict\nSame room also = room conflict
No rejected records, overlaps,\nor unavailable bookings?

title: Advanced Numeric Pattern Generator
statement: Generate a hollow, symmetric numeric diamond for a user-specified number of levels. Validate the dimension, preserve alignment, and handle the single-level boundary without printing a duplicate digit.
objectives: Use nested loops to map rows and columns to a pattern.
Derive the matching upper and lower halves from one level formula.
Print only boundary digits while preserving the hollow interior.
Validate dimensions and report the generated height, width, and digit count.
assumptions: The chosen variant of the brief is a hollow numeric diamond. A level is represented by its own digit.
Accept an integer size from 1 to 9 so every printed value occupies one character.
The output has 2 * size - 1 rows and the same maximum width. Spaces between the two edge digits remain blank.
Rows are shown in a monospaced font. Leading spaces are meaningful; trailing spaces are removed.
Invalid sizes are retried. At size 1, the left and right edges coincide and print one digit.
output: A hollow numeric diamond followed by its height, maximum width, and the number of printed digits.
thinking: Decomposition: validate the size, determine each row's level, determine boundaries, and print.
Pattern recognition: lower-half levels mirror the upper half.
Abstraction: a cell needs only its row, column, and the two edge positions.
Algorithm design: one nested row/column loop handles both halves and the size-one case.
algorithm: Read and validate size between 1 and 9.
Set dimension = 2 * size - 1 and digit count = 0.
For each row from 1 through dimension, use level = row in the upper half and level = 2 * size - row in the lower half.
Calculate left_edge = size - level + 1 and right_edge = size + level - 1.
Scan all columns. Append the level digit when the column matches either edge; otherwise append one space.
Increment the digit count only once for each printed cell, including coincident edges.
Remove trailing spaces and print the completed row.
Print the height, maximum width, and digit count.
pseudocode:
START
READ valid size in 1..9
dimension <- 2 * size - 1
digit_count <- 0
FOR row FROM 1 TO dimension
    IF row <= size: level <- row
    ELSE: level <- 2 * size - row
    left_edge <- size - level + 1
    right_edge <- size + level - 1
    line <- empty string
    FOR column FROM 1 TO dimension
        IF column = left_edge OR column = right_edge
            APPEND text(level) to line
            digit_count <- digit_count + 1
        ELSE
            APPEND one space to line
    REMOVE trailing spaces from line
    PRINT line
PRINT dimension as height and maximum width
PRINT digit_count
STOP
conclusion: A single mirrored level formula generates the complete pattern with basic loops and strings. Tests include both size limits, invalid dimensions, exact row spacing, and the special one-digit output for size 1.

nodes: Take the next row\nStart an empty line
Find mirrored level\nleft = size - level + 1\nright = size + level - 1
Print height, maximum width\nand digit count

title: Password Policy Validation Engine
statement: Evaluate fictional password samples against a declared length, character-category, repetition, and prohibited-substring policy. Report every failed condition for each sample, without repeating the full password in the result audit.
objectives: Scan strings using loops and character comparisons.
Collect every policy failure instead of stopping after the first one.
Detect consecutive character runs and case-insensitive substrings.
Separate input-format errors from password-policy failures.
assumptions: This is a string-processing classroom policy, not a production authentication system. Use fictional sample strings. Normal input() entry is visible in a terminal; only the audit avoids printing full passwords.
Accept 1-20 samples in username|password form, with exactly one separator. Usernames contain 3-20 ASCII letters or digits.
Password length is 10-64 characters. Require at least one ASCII uppercase letter, lowercase letter, digit, and one special character from !@#$%^&*?_-.
Only those character groups are allowed. Password whitespace is preserved and rejected; it is not silently stripped. The pipe character is not an allowed password character.
Three or more identical consecutive characters are prohibited. Repetition matching is case-sensitive.
The substrings password, admin, qwerty, and 1234 are forbidden regardless of case. A valid username must not appear in the password regardless of case.
Malformed records are rejected as samples. For a correctly shaped record, report all independently testable failures. An invalid username does not prevent evaluation of the other password rules.
input: Enter the sample count, then username|password. Example fictional input: Mira|M8!riverOak.
output: Sample number and username, ACCEPTED or REJECTED status, every failed condition, and accepted/rejected totals.
thinking: Decomposition: validate record shape, scan categories, detect runs, and inspect substrings.
Pattern recognition: one scan can collect category flags and run lengths together.
Abstraction: represent compliance through booleans and a list of failure explanations.
Algorithm design: accept only when the full failure list remains empty.
algorithm: Read a valid sample count and initialize result and summary lists/counters.
Split each sample on the separator; reject malformed records.
Check username syntax and password length.
Scan every password character to set category flags, flag disallowed characters, and detect runs of at least three identical characters.
Append a separate failure for each missing category, invalid-character condition, and prohibited run.
Compare a lowercase copy with every prohibited substring and the valid username.
Store the sample number, username, and complete failure list.
Print ACCEPTED for empty failure lists; otherwise print REJECTED and all reasons. Print totals.
pseudocode:
START
READ sample_count in 1..20
DEFINE allowed special characters and prohibited substrings
FOR EACH sample
    failures <- empty list
    READ username|password without trimming password
    IF record does not contain exactly two fields
        ADD malformed-record failure
    ELSE
        CHECK username syntax and password length
        INITIALIZE category flags, run length, and previous character
        FOR EACH character IN password
            SET its ASCII category flag OR flag invalid character
            IF character = previous: increment run length
            ELSE: run length <- 1
            IF run length >= 3: flag prohibited repetition
            previous <- character
        ADD a failure for every missing category
        ADD invalid-character and repetition failures when applicable
        FOR EACH prohibited substring
            IF it appears in lowercase(password): ADD its failure
        IF username is valid AND lowercase(username) appears in lowercase(password)
            ADD username-substring failure
    STORE (sample number, username, failures)
    UPDATE accepted or rejected count
PRINT every sample status and every failure
PRINT totals
STOP
conclusion: The validator explains policy outcomes using only string scans, lists, tuples, and conditionals. Tests cover length limits, every kind of policy rule, case-insensitive matching, preserved whitespace, and the difference between two and three repeated characters.

Read username | password\nStart an empty failure list
Check username and length\nScan character categories and runs\nCollect every failed condition
Check all prohibited substrings\nand username without regard to case
Store sample result and failure list\nEmpty list = accepted\nOtherwise = rejected
Print each status and every failure\nPrint accepted / rejected totals

title: String-Based Examination Answer Evaluation
statement: Compare student answer strings with an answer key. Count correct, incorrect, and unanswered responses, apply positive and negative marking, classify results using stated thresholds, and identify all students tied for the top valid score.
objectives: Validate answer strings before accessing matching character positions.
Use string indexing to count three mutually exclusive response outcomes.
Apply negative marking without silently clamping negative totals.
Handle top-score ties and the case where no valid student record exists.
assumptions: The answer key contains 1-50 letters A-D; letter case is normalized. Accept 1-30 attempted student records.
Student IDs contain 1-12 ASCII letters or digits and normalize to uppercase. A correctly shaped row with a valid new ID reserves the ID even if its answer string is invalid.
Each response string has exactly the key length and contains A-D or '-' for unanswered. Outer whitespace is stripped; interior whitespace is invalid.
Correct = +4 marks, incorrect = -1, unanswered = 0. Final scores may be negative. Maximum score = 4 * question_count.
Percentage = score * 100 / maximum. At least 75% gives DISTINCTION, at least 50% gives PASS, otherwise NEEDS PRACTICE.
Malformed student records count as attempts and are excluded from scores and ranking. All top-score ties are shown in input order.
input: Enter the answer key, record count, and ID|responses for each student. Example: S02|AB-D for key ABCD.
output: Rejected-record reasons; correct, incorrect, and unanswered counts; score, percentage and classification; evaluation totals; and top-score ties.
thinking: Decomposition: validate the key, validate each record, score positions, and rank.
Pattern recognition: each character position produces exactly one response outcome.
Abstraction: an answer string is an ordered list of symbols, not free-form text.
Algorithm design: initialize the maximum below the lowest possible score so all-negative results still rank correctly.
algorithm: Read and validate a nonempty key containing only A-D, then a valid student record count.
Validate each record's shape and unique ID, then its response length and permitted symbols.
For every answer position, count '-' as unanswered, an equal symbol as correct, and any other permitted symbol as incorrect.
Calculate score = 4 * correct - incorrect and percentage against the maximum.
Assign the classification using the 75% and 50% boundaries.
Store valid result tuples and print reasons for invalid records.
Print valid results and track the highest score, retaining all ties.
If none are valid, explicitly report that no top score is available.
pseudocode:
START
READ a valid answer_key of 1..50 symbols A-D
READ student_count in 1..30
seen_ids <- empty list; results <- empty list
FOR EACH attempted student record
    READ ID and responses; normalize letter case
    VALIDATE record, new ID, exact length, and symbols A-D or '-'
    RESERVE syntactically valid IDs in correctly shaped records
    IF invalid: PRINT reason and increment rejected
    ELSE
        correct <- 0; incorrect <- 0; unanswered <- 0
        FOR position FROM 0 TO key length - 1
            IF responses[position] = '-': increment unanswered
            ELSE IF responses[position] = key[position]: increment correct
            ELSE: increment incorrect
        score <- 4 * correct - incorrect
        percentage <- score * 100 / (4 * key length)
        IF percentage >= 75: classification <- DISTINCTION
        ELSE IF percentage >= 50: classification <- PASS
        ELSE: classification <- NEEDS PRACTICE
        APPEND result tuple
highest <- -(key length) - 1
FOR EACH result: PRINT result and UPDATE highest score and ties
PRINT evaluated and rejected counts
IF results is empty: PRINT no valid top score
ELSE: PRINT highest score and all tied IDs
STOP
conclusion: The scoring rules account for every response exactly once, including blanks and negative totals. Tests demonstrate correct threshold classifications, lowercase normalization, all-negative ranking, and a safe result when every record is invalid.

title: Student Marks Matrix Analysis
statement: Analyze a matrix of student marks across subjects. Calculate student totals and averages, determine classifications using subject-wise passing requirements, calculate subject totals, averages and extrema, identify tied top performers, and flag subjects with low average performance.
objectives: Represent marks as a validated rectangular nested list.
Traverse the matrix by rows for student statistics and by columns for subject statistics.
Keep subject-wise pass criteria separate from average-based classifications.
Report all top-score ties and subjects below a specified average.
assumptions: Accept 1-20 students and 1-10 subjects. Marks are whole numbers from 0 to 100, inclusive.
Subject codes and student IDs contain 1-12 ASCII letters or digits, normalize to uppercase, and must be unique within their respective lists.
Invalid subject lists and student rows are retried. The matrix is not analyzed until every requested row is valid and complete.
A mark of at least 40 is required in every subject. Any lower mark makes the student FAIL regardless of average.
Among students passing every subject: average >= 75 gives DISTINCTION; average >= 60 gives FIRST CLASS; all remaining passing averages give PASS.
A subject is flagged when its class average is strictly below 50. Exactly 50 is not flagged.
Overall top performers are determined by total marks across all valid students, independent of pass classification. Subject toppers use that subject's mark. Every tie is retained in input order.
input: Enter student count, subject count, a pipe-separated subject-code list, then ID|mark1|...|markN for each student.
output: Student totals, averages, failed subjects and classifications; subject totals, averages, lowest/highest marks and toppers; overall top ties, overall average, and low-average subject labels.
thinking: Decomposition: validate matrix dimensions, calculate rows, calculate columns, and summarize.
Pattern recognition: the same aggregation pattern applies to each row and each column.
Abstraction: keep student identifiers and subject labels separate from the numeric matrix.
Algorithm design: use nested index loops so each mark is attributed to its correct student and subject.
algorithm: Read valid student and subject counts.
Read a complete unique subject-code list; retry malformed lists.
Read student rows, validating ID uniqueness, exact mark count, and the 0-100 range.
Append each accepted ID and its marks list to parallel identifier and matrix lists.
For each row, sum marks, identify failed subjects, calculate the average, and apply classification rules.
Track the highest total and all tied student IDs while accumulating the grand total.
For each column, calculate total, average, minimum, maximum, and all subject toppers.
Flag averages below 50 and print the overall average, overall top ties, and weak subjects.
pseudocode:
START
READ student_count in 1..20 and subject_count in 1..10
READ exactly subject_count unique valid subject codes; RETRY errors
student_ids <- empty list; marks_matrix <- empty nested list
WHILE accepted students < student_count
    READ ID and subject_count marks
    CHECK new valid ID, correct row length, and integer marks 0..100
    IF invalid: PRINT error; RETRY
    ELSE: APPEND ID and the marks row
FOR EACH student row
    total <- 0; failed_subjects <- empty list
    FOR EACH subject column
        ADD mark to total
        IF mark < 40: APPEND subject label to failed_subjects
    average <- total / subject_count
    IF failed_subjects is not empty: classification <- FAIL
    ELSE IF average >= 75: classification <- DISTINCTION
    ELSE IF average >= 60: classification <- FIRST CLASS
    ELSE: classification <- PASS
    PRINT row statistics; UPDATE highest total and ties
    ADD total to grand_total
FOR EACH subject column
    SCAN all rows for total, minimum, maximum, and all maximum ties
    average <- total / student_count
    IF average < 50: APPEND subject to weak_subjects
    PRINT column statistics
PRINT overall top ties
PRINT grand_total / (student_count * subject_count)
PRINT weak_subjects or none
STOP
conclusion: The validated matrix supports both student and subject analysis without external libraries. Tests cover one-cell matrices, zero and full marks, exact classification thresholds, a failed subject despite a high average, and all forms of tied top scores.

title: Tuple-Based Product Catalogue Audit
statement: Store product identifiers, unit prices, stock, and reorder levels as tuples. Audit malformed and duplicate records, calculate product and total inventory values, and identify the items and quantities requiring replenishment.
objectives: Validate structured product identifiers and decimal-price strings.
Convert prices into integer paise using only string and integer operations.
Store immutable product records in tuples and unpack them for analysis.
Exclude invalid records from inventory valuation and replenishment totals.
assumptions: Accept 1-30 attempted records. Product IDs normalize to uppercase and must be P followed by exactly three ASCII digits.
The first correctly shaped row with a syntactically valid new ID reserves that ID, even if a later price or stock check fails. Repeated IDs are rejected.
Prices are positive rupee amounts with a required integer part and optionally one or two decimal places: 12, 12.5, and 12.50 are valid; .50, 1., negatives, and excess precision are invalid.
Convert prices to integer paise. Inventory arithmetic stays in paise; rupee conversion is only for display.
Stock and reorder level are nonnegative whole units. A zero reorder level is permitted.
Replenishment is reorder_level - stock when stock is lower, otherwise zero. Stock equal to the reorder level does not trigger replenishment.
Invalid records count as attempts but contribute to neither inventory value nor replenishment. The report shows the first validation error for each rejected row.
input: Enter the record count, then Pddd|price_in_Rs|stock|reorder_level. Example: P002|3.75|2|8.
output: Rejected-record reasons; each valid product's unit price, stock, inventory value and replenishment; total value; total units needed; and item IDs below their reorder levels.
thinking: Decomposition: validate identity, parse the price, validate quantities, and value inventory.
Pattern recognition: every valid tuple supports the same stock-times-price calculation.
Abstraction: use integer paise so decimal-input formatting does not control arithmetic accuracy.
Algorithm design: reject invalid records before appending typed tuples to the catalogue.
algorithm: Read a valid record count and initialize the catalogue, seen IDs, and rejection count.
Validate four fields and the Pddd identifier; reject repeated IDs and reserve each new valid ID.
Split the price around the decimal point, require a digit-only integer part and at most two fractional digits, and pad a single fractional digit with zero.
Convert whole rupees and fractional paise to one positive integer price.
Validate stock and reorder level as nonnegative integers, then append the typed product tuple.
For each valid tuple, calculate value = unit_price_paise * stock.
Calculate the replenishment gap, retain below-level product IDs, and accumulate value and unit totals.
Print the catalogue audit, rejection count, total value, and replenishment summary.
pseudocode:
START
READ record_count in 1..30
catalogue <- empty list; seen_ids <- empty list
FOR EACH attempted record
    READ ID, price_text, stock_text, reorder_text
    CHECK four fields, Pddd ID format, and uniqueness
    RESERVE every new syntactically valid ID
    SPLIT price_text on decimal point
    REQUIRE one or two parts and an ASCII integer part
    IF a fraction is present: REQUIRE one or two ASCII digits
    PAD one fractional digit to two; absent fraction becomes 00
    price_paise <- integer_part * 100 + fractional_paise
    CHECK price_paise > 0 and nonnegative whole stock/reorder values
    IF valid: APPEND (ID, price_paise, stock, reorder_level)
    ELSE: PRINT reason; increment rejected
inventory_value <- 0; replenishment_units <- 0
FOR EACH (ID, price_paise, stock, reorder_level) IN catalogue
    value <- price_paise * stock
    replenish <- 0
    IF stock < reorder_level
        replenish <- reorder_level - stock
        RECORD ID for replenishment
    ACCUMULATE value and replenish
    PRINT product values formatted in rupees
PRINT valid/rejected counts, total value, units needed, and item IDs
STOP
conclusion: The catalogue audit uses tuple records and integer money calculations to produce a repeatable inventory report. Tests cover one-paise prices, one-digit fractions, exact reorder boundaries, invalid decimal formats, and duplicate IDs following rejected records.
